name: Cisco
summary: Cisco says its interview process varies by team and role, and that engineering roles typically include a behavioral interview and a technical assessment, such as a coding test. Candidates commonly report questions on networking fundamentals, operating systems and coding for software roles, and Cisco's careers site sets out how candidates may, and may not, use generative AI during hiring.
rounds: Online application; recruiters check your résumé against the minimum qualifications
Recruiter conversation about the role and your background
Technical or pre-employment assessment for some positions, such as a coding test
Technical interviews: networking, coding, systems and your projects, depending on the role
Behavioral interview, often with the hiring manager
looks_for: Networking fundamentals: the TCP/IP and OSI models, routing, switching and common protocols
Collaboration, which Cisco's careers site calls how it gets things done
Your own thinking and experience, not scripted answers
Coding and problem solving for software roles
Security awareness in how you design and run systems

questions.text: Tell me about a time you worked across teams to solve a customer's problem.
covers: The customer's problem and which teams were involved
How you coordinated and kept the customer informed
The outcome, ideally with a measurable result

questions.text: Tell me about something you taught yourself recently, such as a certification or a new tool, and why you chose it.
covers: What you learned and what prompted it
How you learned it: labs, projects, study plan
Where you've already used it

questions.text: Tell me about a time you took the initiative on something that wasn't assigned to you.
covers: What you noticed that others hadn't acted on
What you did and who you involved
The result and what it led to

questions.text: Tell me about a time a change you made caused a problem. How did you handle it?
covers: The change and the problem it caused
How you responded: rolled back, told people, fixed it
What you now do before making changes

questions.text: Explain, layer by layer, what happens when one computer sends data to another on a different network.
covers: Application data wrapped into TCP or UDP, then IP packets, then frames
ARP for the next hop, switching locally and routing between networks
DNS lookups and how the receiving side unwraps each layer

questions.text: What's the difference between TCP and UDP, and when would you choose each?
covers: Connection, ordering, reliability and congestion control in TCP
Low overhead and no delivery guarantees in UDP
Examples: file transfer and web pages versus live voice, video or DNS

questions.text: How does a router decide where to send a packet, and how do static routes differ from protocols like OSPF or BGP?
covers: The routing table and longest-prefix match
Static routes set by hand versus routes learned dynamically
OSPF inside an organisation versus BGP between networks

questions.text: Users in one office can reach the internet but not an internal application. How would you troubleshoot it?
covers: Narrowing the scope: which users, since when, from where
Working through layers: DNS, routing, firewall rules, VPN or the application itself
Confirming the fix and recording what changed

questions.text: What are VLANs, and why would a network team use them?
covers: Logically separate networks on shared switches
Uses: security, smaller broadcast domains, organising by team or function
Trunk ports and routing between VLANs

questions.text: How would you design a system that collects health data from thousands of network devices and alerts on problems?
covers: Collecting metrics by streaming or polling, and storing them as time series
Alert rules that catch real problems without flooding people
Scaling the collectors and handling devices that go silent

questions.text: How would you secure access to company systems for staff working from home?
covers: Strong identity: multi-factor authentication and checking device health
Least-privilege access per application rather than open network access
Monitoring, logging, and a plan for lost or compromised devices

questions.text: How would you improve video call quality for participants on poor connections?
covers: Adapting video quality to available bandwidth and protecting audio first
Jitter buffers, error correction and choosing nearby media servers
Measuring quality from the user's side and testing on bad networks

questions.text: Why Cisco, and which part of its business (networking, security, collaboration or observability) interests you most?
covers: A specific area and what you know about it
A link to your skills, certifications or projects
What you want to learn there

questions.text: What questions do you have for us about the team or the role?
covers: Questions about the team's customers and current challenges
How success is measured in the first months
Learning and growth opportunities in the role

tips: Cisco's recruiters suggest listing professional certifications on your résumé; be ready to explain what you learned from each.
Revise networking from the ground up: subnetting, the TCP handshake, DNS, DHCP, routing and switching.
Cisco's hiring page allows AI for things like readability checks and prep tips, but not for scripted answers, assessment responses or real-time coding or design solutions.
Prepare questions for your interviewers; Cisco's careers site encourages candidates to ask about the company, team and role.
Read Cisco customer stories and blogs for the area you're applying to; its early-careers page suggests this.
